awd_titl_txt: EAGER: Exploratory Study of Hybrid Quantum Encoding in Ring Multicore Fibers at Visible Wavelengths
awd_abstract_narration:
This project investigates a new approach to quantum photonics by leveraging specialty optical fibers, originally designed for telecommunication, as compact platforms for advanced quantum information encoding. By exploring these fibers at visible wavelengths, where they behave differently than their design specifications, the project opens new possibilities for encoding quantum information using both spatial and particle properties of light. This work addresses the national interest by advancing foundational science in quantum technologies which are key areas for future secure communication, precision measurement, and quantum computing. In addition to scientific advancement, the project fosters interdisciplinary education, providing hands-on training for students in quantum optics, integrated photonics, and machine learning-based data analysis. Public outreach activities, in collaboration with the Buffalo Amateur Astronomy Association, will further broaden public understanding of quantum technologies.

Technical Project Description
The proposed research aims to explore the use of interacting ring-shaped multicore optical fibers (MCFs) at visible wavelengths to develop new hybrid quantum encoding schemes. Operating these telecom-grade fibers outside their design parameters at visible wavelengths enables the investigation of spatial mode structures for quantum light which is an area largely unexplored. By integrating MCFs with quantum light sources and photon-counting detectors, the project will demonstrate encoding of quantum information in high-dimensional Hilbert spaces, essential for scalable quantum communication and computing. The research involves simulations of quantum dynamics in MCFs, experimental validation of hybrid qudit-based encoding, and real-time machine learning-based photon classification. Additionally, the project will study inter-core coupling dynamics to realize quantum random walks and Boson Sampling in a fiber-based platform. These experiments aim to demonstrate new architectures for near-term quantum advantage. This exploratory effort will lay the groundwork for scalable, low-loss, fiber-integrated quantum devices, representing a paradigm shift in quantum photonic integration.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
What if the ordinary fiber-optic cables that already carry the world's internet could also carry quantum information? This exploratory project, a collaboration between the University at Buffalo and Corning Incorporated, showed that they can, and in a way that had not been demonstrated before.

Quantum technologies promise fundamentally new capabilities in computing and secure communication, but they need hardware that can transport fragile quantum signals. Multicore fibers, strands of glass with many parallel light-guiding channels, were developed by industry to push more internet traffic through a single cable. We asked whether this mass-produced telecom technology could serve quantum science directly.

Using a 39-core fiber manufactured by Corning, our team demonstrated, to our knowledge for the first time, that three independent quantum properties of light can be measured simultaneously in such a fiber: how many photons arrive, what spatial shape the light takes inside a core, and which core it travels through. Each of these properties can carry information, so reading all three at once multiplies the capacity for quantum encoding in a cable technology that is already manufactured at industrial scale.

Two further findings stand out. Individual photons keep their delicate quantum character while traveling through the fiber, so each core can host a true quantum bit encoded in the internal shape of the light. And the fiber turned out to have a built-in control: simply shifting the point where light enters changes how strongly neighboring cores exchange light, by roughly a factor of three, with no electronics or moving parts. Reconfigurable quantum circuits normally require costly active components; here the standard fiber provides the adjustment for free. The project also established a precisely calibrated baseline that other laboratories can use to certify genuine quantum effects in similar systems, along with a warning about a subtle data-analysis pitfall that can imitate them.

This project shows what an industry-university partnership can do that neither side could do alone. Corning contributed the specialty fiber and scientific expertise; the University at Buffalo contributed the quantum measurement capability; and the results were published jointly, with a Corning scientist as co-author. The work is openly available as a preprint (arXiv:2610.03493) and is under review at a peer-reviewed journal, and the measurement methods developed here form the basis for future joint work on much larger systems. The partnership also connects quantum research and student training in Upstate New York with regional industry.

The award trained two graduate students and two undergraduate students in experimental quantum optics; both undergraduates contributed strongly enough to become co-authors of the publication. Beyond the university, the team brought quantum science to the public through a continuing partnership with the Buffalo Amateur Astronomy Association, including a public lecture on the physics of light and a hands-on quantum cryptography activity at Chestnut Ridge Park that reached several hundred visitors, who encrypted and cracked secret messages using the same rules of quantum physics that protect future communication networks. The interactive materials built for that event remain freely available online for anyone to use.
